div.p: The extent of May celebrations in Aston Abbotts is not well understood. In his household book, Sir Edward Don of Horsenden alludes to a murder that took place at the 'Astun' May game in 1527. Don does not make clear the circumstances for the game or the murder, and it is also not clear whether 'Astun' refers to Aston Abbotts, Aston Clinton, Aston Sandford, or with another similarly named location in Buckinghamshire.

div.p: Seventeenth-century Buckinghamshire was home to numerous inns called The Bell, including ones in Winslow, Chearsley, Long Crendon, and Hardwick, all of which are now listed buildings. In Aylesbury, a still-extant pub called The Bell was constructed in the nineteenth century. Its façade conceals an older structure; however, no precise date is provided in the official list entry for the Aylesbury Bell ('The Bell Hotel, Market Square,' Historic England: National Heritage List for England, , accessed 23 August 2026).

div.p: John Borlase (c1527-93) of Little Marlow, Buckinghamshire, was JP for Buckinghamshire from 1573 and MP in 1586. He was sheriff for Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire 1567-8, and for Buckinghamshire 1588-9. div.p: In 1524 Sir Edward embarked on a two-month journey from Buckinghamshire to Wales. He left on 20 August with about ten horses and a large retinue of servants. The group covered about 25 to 30 miles a day and arrived in Wales around late September.

Sir Edward received an entry fine from Walter Collins (f 108, 11 October), a relative of one of Sir Edward's servants, for occupying a house near Kidwelly on 6 October. In turn, Sir Edward paid Collins' harper on 11 October. The payment to a harper on 12 October occurred at the house of Morgan Tailor, former bailiff of Carmarthen (Griffiths, 'Travelling,' pp 5– 6, 9).

In 1524, Sir Edward embarked on a two-month journey from Buckinghamshire to Wales. The payment to a harper on 12 October (f 108) occurred at the house of Morgan Tailor, former bailiff of Carmarthen (Griffiths, 'Travelling,' pp 5–6, 9).

From the context of this entry (f 113) it appears that Sir Edward was spending a few days shopping for himself in Uxbridge, a town in Middlesex on the London road where members of the household frequently shopped.

div.ab: Item the xxiij day gevyn to the mynsterels xvj d.

div.p: This is a baffling reference (f 114) on the 'memo' page for 1527. William Mede, a member of the Horsenden household, appears often in subsequent accounts so he was clearly not the murder victim. The series of items on this page are written as one paragraph, not separated as the expense items most frequently are line by line. 'dyd kyll' ends a line and 'wylliam mede' begins the next line. Sir Edward realized his mistake and went back and inserted (with a carat mark) in the left hand margin beside 'wylliam' an illegible name. Griffiths reads the illegible word as 'Culenton' and identifies it as the village of Calverton (Griffiths, Household Book, p 126; p 468).

However, Calverton is located in the northern part of the county near Stony Stratford and certainly not on the road to London from Horsenden. Similarly, none of the three Buckinghamshire villages using the word Aston (Aston Abbotts, Aston Clinton or Aston Tirrold) would have taken Mede to a road to London. What seems more likely is that Sir Edward, as he often did, was speaking of two separate events in this memo. The illegible word must be the name of Bennett's victim noting the first event and the second that Mede went to a may game at Aston Rowant, a village close to Horsenden just over the Oxfordshire border close to the nearest road to London through Uxbridge. However, there are multiple locations called Aston throughout the county, and May game records are attested only in Aston Abbotts .
This account is bound out of order coming after the November accounts. Sir Edward, Lady Don and their son-in-law, Thomas Johns (Jones), were in Langley, near Windsor when this payment was made.

row.cell: Item for E don a papete

div.p: The other members of the family besides Sir Edward himself with names beginning with 'E' were Sir Edward's daughter Elizabeth, who was an adult, married and about to have her second child. Sir Edward's brother, Sir Gruffydd, also had a daughter Elizabeth but she would also have been an adult by 1528 (Griffiths, Household Book, p xxxiii). It is unlikely to be Sir Edward himself because he always referred to himself with a personal pronoun and this entry would have read 'Item for a papete for me.' For example, on f 124 in the account for November 1527 he noted 'Item for iij payer of shoys for me ij s. viij d.' but 'Item a knyffe for e don ij d.'

div.p: The entry payment to Thomas may have taken place in Aylesbury. On Thursday, 12 January, after his morning shave for which he paid the usual 4d, he spent 2d in Wendover (possibly for a small lunch) and arrived in Aylesbury in time for his supper which cost him 13d with wine for 3d. The next day he went to the Franciscan friary where he heard mass and contributed to the friary. The evening expenses that included the payment to the fool seem to have been for a convivial affair where he was staying the night and provided 'dyners and sopers,' sack, a fire and candle with ale. It is not clear whether he was entertaining some of the friars or other friends living in Aylesbury but Thomas seems to have provided the show for the evening. Sir Edward was back in Horsenden the next day, Saturday, 14 January (all on f 177v, see Griffiths, Household Book, p 206).

div.head: f 203 (25 February)
div.ab: ther cam with theyme the syngyng glover as on the last day they departyd

div.p: f 203: This is part of the last entry in the 'Memorandum' page for February 1532/3. The 'theyme' referred to were a man and a woman from London who came to the area around Princes Risborough to gamble. They stayed at Coleshill, then part of the manor of Ranes held by the Brudenell family (VCH: Buckinghamshire, vol 3, pp 141–155, British History Online, https://www.british- history.ac.uk/vch/bucks/vol3/pp141-155, accessed 25 July 2026). Sir Robert Brudenell (1461–1531), who had died two years earlier, came from a Buckinghamshire family with land near Amersham and had been a judge. According to Sir Edward, two constables came and found them 'playng at the cardys for money.' They bribed one of the constables, Johan Bollen, 1s 4d, and the constables went away (f 203v). The 'singing glover' is not mentioned in the accounts for the month of February.

div.p: 'p{r}incsces' (f 213v) must refer to Henry Fitzroy (1519–36), duke of Richmond and Somerset, Henry VIII's illegitimate son by his mistress Elizabeth Blount. 1533 was the year Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon was declared illegal and Princess Mary declared illegitimate. At this time there was talk of Henry Fitzroy being named heir to the throne. King Henry formally married Anne Boleyn on 25 January 1532/3, but Elizabeth was not born until 7 September. At the date of this performance, Henry had two acknowledged illegitimate children – Mary and Henry Fitzroy. The male child was favoured to be the heir if the child Anne was carrying did not live.

Fitzroy was raised in Sheriff Hutton Castle in Yorkshire, North Riding, about ten miles north of York. Numerous tour stops are recorded for Fitzroy's players in 1533; see P&P; James H. Forse, 'Advertising Status and Legitimacy: or, Why Did Henry VIII's Queens and Children Patronize Travelling Performers?,' Early Theatre 16.2 (2013), p 70.
Folio 214 is torn down a fold line. Wendover is a parish south of Aylesbury about seven miles northeast of Horsenden.

div.p: Maxwell-Lyte cites this statute and translates it (History of Eton, p 153); he renders 'preter misse secreta' as 'sacred portions of the mass' rather than 'secret prayers of the mass.' The excerpt is preceded by a statute concerning the greater double feasts, and lays down who should officiate and how the feasts should be conducted. Then comes this exception for the one unusual greater double feast – the feast of St Nicholas (6 December), when the boy bishop was elected for the day.

div.p: The Feast of the Circumcision is 1 January, still within the twelve days of the Christmas festival. The Feast of the Circumcision could also be the occasion for celebrating the Feast of Fools. Feast of Fools traditions were primarily prevalent in France, with only scattered examples in England, but they did overlap with boy bishop traditions. For more on English examples of the Feast of Fools and their overlap with Boy Bishop ceremonies, see Max Harris, Sacred Folly: A New History of the Feast of Fools (Cornell University Press, 2011), pp 172–180). According to the Eton College Statutes, however, the boy bishops traditions were to be celebrated on December 6.

div.p: Andrew Windsor (1467-1542) was first Baron Windsor from 1529; see P&P. Originally from Middlesex, he acquired a lease at Bradenham, Buckinghamshire around 1505 (HPO, ht tps://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1509- 1558/member/windsor-sir-andrew-1467-1543, accessed 22 October 2026). His son, William Windsor (1498-1558), was second Baron Windsor from 1542, with residence at Bradenham, Buckinghamshire; see P&P. The younger Windsor is known to have patronized players in Lyme Regis, Dorset in 1552–3, so it is possible that Eton borrowed the costumes from him rather than from his father.
Nicholas Udall (1504–56) became headmaster of Eton in 1534 (Matthew Steggle, 'Udall Yevedale, Nicholas (1504–1556),' ODNB, accessed 10 October 2026).

div.p: The inventory at the end of Audit Book 4 is dated 1570-1 by both Motter, School Drama, pp 259-60, and Blewitt, 'Winchester and Eton [pt 2],' p 139, because of its place in this set of accounts. James, in a more detailed study, relates the inventory to other material also in the manuscript dated 1595; see Etoniana, p 512). This edition follows James' dating because of his more intimate knowledge of the accounts and the life of the college.

The ambiguity of the date makes it difficult to pinpoint which headmaster held these items. If the account is from 1570–1, then the headmaster may have been William Malim. By most accounts, William Malim (1533–1594) was headmaster from 1561 to 1563; however, Sterry claims his tenure lasted until 1571 (Stephen Wright, 'Malym Malim, William (1533–1594),' ODNB, accessed 21 October 2026; Sterry, Eton College Register, p xxxii)).

If the account is indeed from 1595, then the headmaster would have been either John Hammond or Richard Langley, who held the post from 1583–94 and 1594–1611 respectively (Sterry, Eton College Register, p xxxii).

div.p: Edward Wooden was churchwarden in 1616 and 1618-19. On f 37 there appears a memo signed by him and his fellow warden John Sanders and the vicar, Anthony Watson. On f 40v there is an entry concerning the proceeds of the ale held during his tenure. He apparently took the morris gear home with him after his time as churchwarden. Wooden is specifically recorded as paying the church nine pounds rent for a house in the church close in 1624-5 (f 49v). Rent for some property in the church close is taken over by a man called Neville in 1630 (f 60). In that year all mention of the morris equipment disappears from the records. Presumably Wooden gave over the equipment that year and Neville rented the property he had held. The last mention of Wooden appears in 1636 (f 80) where the 'Widow Wooden' has not paid 6s 8d for her husband's grave. Wooden is referred to as a brewer in property records from around the time when he served as churchwarden (Buckinghamshire Archives, D-CE/M/67; Buckinghamshire Archives, D-BAS/60/178 .

div.head: ff [1-1v] (8 November)
div.ab:
Of that Tumult at Olney, or what part the Vicar had there in, I never heard anye thinge but by your Letter. Indeed the Vicar came vnto me, in the Companye of a Doctor of Divinitie his Alliesman, and in his hearinge, I did (at two severall dayes) spend some time, in lettinge him see, that hee ought in Conscience, and might with all sagetie obey the Commaund of his Lawfull Superior (and much more the Kinges) in the publication of this Booke ,which (as I endeavour'd to shewe) contayned some thinges, much conduceinge to the encrease of pietie & devotion, and nothinge clearelye opposite to Godes Worde. And for the contingent abuse that ille people maye hereafter make thereof; hee ought in Charitie to beleeve that the kinge is as wise to foresee, and wilbe (vpon the first discouerye) as willinge to redresse the same as anye private man of the Clergye or Laytie can or pretende of himselfe. But to require his Approbation vnto the Booke (as was done to the .3. Articles) I therefore omitted, because it is not either by the booke itselfe or any Lawe or Commaund of the Kinges, or Letter of my Lords Grace the Metropolitan, soe of me required. And I doe measure the
Obedience of my Clergye by Actinge rather then allowinge what in this Kinde they are Commaunded. If you knowe it, to be otherwise conceived by those that are better vers't then I am in these particulars, you maye doe (without anye offence vnto me) what you please, in your own independent Iurisdiction.

div.p: This letter is signed by John Lincoln.
In 1635, the vicar of Olney, William Worcester, had to sign a declaration that he had read the King's Book of Sports and accepted it as lawful (TNA: SP 16/308 f 48).

div.head: ff [1-2] (5 November)
div.ab: Right reuerend my Good Lord

I hold yt fitte in my duty & respect to your honour to acqainte your Lordship with some proceedinges in this Archdeaconry of Buckingham where I am officiall. Coming from Trinity tearme I understood of a late tumult at olney. Some daunced after evening prayer on a Sunday the vicar raised vp the constable & others with billes & holbertes against them much a doe there was & godes great blessing that more mischeif was not done. I called the Vicar & finding him averse against the kinges booke of recreacions I moniced monished him to read yt which he refused & I suspended him about jo Iuli last & that he should ‸not easily gett an Inhibicion from the Arches or Audiencein this sicknes time when few remaine there but Clerkes, I added my power of Deane of the Arches also in the Act; I hard since that he had vowed to his refractary company yat ‸he would never read yt: and I found that hee sought all meanes wayes to shuffle yt of: first he would haue the cure served by his Curate & himself continew obstinate & yett haue all the profittes vppon which I moniced his Curate to read the booke which he also refused and him I suspended & he is Run out of the country. Then the Vicar practised to secure himselfe of the stipend and lett the cure be served as yt might. So the cure was at an ill stay standing so longe voide that people stood at a gaze the example was pernicious the kinge dishonored as if he had sett forth an order by that booke that might not with a good conscience be read much lesse obeyed. To avoid that & reforme the Vicar I decreed processe for him about the beginning of octobre to shew cause why crescentente contumacia et obstinacia continuantecrescentente … continuante: 'with contunamcy increasing and obstinance continuing' he should not be further proceeded against as to excomunicacion or amocion from his benefice. This frighted him & sent him to your Lordship whence returning he appeared at his day 19o octobre & said he had received satisfacion from your Lordship
by by: also as catch word at foot of previous folio greater reasons & argumentes then euer he heard before & desired but till the next Court to consider of your Lordships reasons and that then he would conforme; I was glad of yt comended and encouraged him & much honored your Lordship (as my duty was) in open court for so good a worke. And after I vnderstood he had read the booke on a holiday jo November which also he certified before me in court 4o November I was glad of yt gaue him good advise to continew in obedience & vsed this speach Tu autem conversus confirma fratres tuosTu … tuos: 'You, moreover, having been converted, must support your brothers.' Cp Luke 22:32. At which he startled & expressed himself that he was not converted in any thing he onely read the booke to obey your Lordships commandd: many wordes were multiplied whereby I found It ‸he equivocated and dissembled with your Lordship and abused the king & the law; he read yt in deed to lett the people see how ill yt was not that he thought yt lawfull or approved of yt he would not say so in plaine tearmes but all his altercacion in open court ‸tended thereto & so was vnderstood uppon which I admonished him to declare himself to his people in the Church: that as he had readread: r altered froms yt in obedience to your Lordships comaund so he also approued of yt and held yt lawfull to be obeyed: what he will doe, I knowe not; That I used also my power of deane of the Arches I did yt for the cause aboue said and as yt is lawfull by the priveledge of the Church of Canterbury to which I am sworne to & I thinke your Lordship is so too, and it is not prohibited by the statute of Henry the :8: because wee call noe man out of his dioces yett I haue bene ever sparing in your Lordships dioces & in others except in London where wee doe yt continually, so long as wee are within the dioces. div.p: The Conquest of the West Indies (f 1) was a play belonging to the Admiral's Men, printed in 1601 (Martin Wiggins, with Catherine Richardson, British Drama, vol 4: 1598–1602 (Oxford, 2014); Lost Plays Database https://lostplays.folger.edu/Conquest_of_the_West_Indies,_The, accessed 30 June 2026). Philip Henslowe's correspondence about buying and producing the play also dates to 1601, which raises the question of whether Temple was purchasing the play text or a copy of Thomas Nicolls' The Pleasant Historie of the Conquest of the West India, the most likely source text for the play. Thomas Nicolls translated López de Gómara's 1552 Historia de las Indias y Conquista de Mexico into English in 1578 and reprinted the text in 1596. Handes' entry from the autumn of 1600 records that Thomas Temple paid 15d for something to do with the play. If this was simply the entry fee to see the play it seems rather expensive given Temple's payments for other events.

Throughout their marriage, Thomas Temple and his wife Hester lived in various locations, including Stowe, Wolverton, Biddlesden, and Statonbury (all in Buckinghamshire) as well as Burton Dasseett and locations in Warwickshire and Oxfordshire (O'Day, Elite Family, p 39). However, the most likely location for the play at St Paul's would be St Paul's Churchyard in London, where Temple also frequently stayed. See EMLOT.

lg.l: The wisest men haue tride what follie meant
Still to bee laughinge, soe that true content
seem'd to bee onelie hers, soe folly can
laugh out, though fortune frowne, whilst ye wise man
sinks deepe in sorrow, wee are not content
with the example, but th'experiment;
wee'de try our selues, and were resolu'd to night
to foole a little for our owne delight.
But seeing all yow heere, faith wee'wee': apostrophe otiose haue at mind
to please yow too: and the world being enclind
Soe vnto foolerie, sure yow cannot choose
but like of that, which is soe much in vse
It is ye fashion, the trim gallant hee
that with his Taylor plodds for braverie
learnes Cringes of his Monsiur, takes greate paines
for an affected garb, praie whats his gaines
but to bee laught at, hee that doth dispise
all fashions thereby to bee knowne more wise
in his trunk hose, and high crown hatt appeares
an object as ridiculus; though his eares
glow not att all men say; Poets that strive
least after fashions, yet at this arive
soone as the rest, whilst they expose theire witt
to the same purpose, whither wise men sitt
or fooles, as Iudges, of it, theyre best pay
is to bee laught att, wee as wise as they
expect noe more; tis laughter wee intend
and if yow share in't with's, wee haue our end
yet does not laugh too loud, for then I doubt
w'are but young Actors, and youle put vs out.

lg.l: Now wee haue done, and yow haue seene our play
